lead: Small transformers and inductors need a high switching frequency, but every hard-switched transition burns energy while voltage and current overlap. Resonant converters place an inductor and capacitor around the switch and time the gate to the tank's zero crossings, so the device turns on at zero voltage or turns off at zero current. The loss per transition falls, the heatsink shrinks, and frequencies of hundreds of kilohertz become practical. You meet the idea in phone and laptop adapters, TV supplies and server power shelves.
prereq: You need: switching loss, output capacitance and heat-sink ideas from Unit 1, and the PWM cells of Chapters 3.3 to 3.5.

sections.h3: Hard switching sets a frequency ceiling

blocks.text: In a PWM converter the switch is told to change state while it holds the full load voltage and carries the full load current. For the short overlap time the device is neither off nor on: voltage falls while current rises, or current falls while voltage rises. That overlap is the hard-switching loss.
P_sw = ½ · V · I · (t_r + t_f) · f_s
blocks.where: V is the off-state voltage in volts (V); I is the on-state current in amperes (A); t_r is the turn-on overlap time in seconds (s); t_f is the turn-off overlap time in seconds (s); f_s is the switching frequency in hertz (Hz). The ½ assumes a triangular voltage-current overlap.

blocks.text: Two more terms appear every cycle. A diode that turns off must sweep out its stored charge Q_rr, costing about P_rr = Q_rr · V · f_s, where Q_rr is the reverse-recovery charge in coulombs (C). The device output capacitance C_oss stores ½·C_oss·V² and dumps it each cycle, costing P_C = ½ · C_oss · V² · f_s, where C_oss is in farads (F).

Conduction loss is separate: P_cond = I_rms² · R_on, where I_rms is the root-mean-square device current in amperes (A) and R_on is the on-resistance in ohms (Ω). The total is P_total = P_cond + P_sw + P_rr + P_C. At low f_s the conduction term dominates and is roughly constant. Above some frequency the switching terms rise in proportion to f_s, so P_total has a minimum at a best frequency. Plain PWM pushed past that minimum gets hot faster than the magnetics shrink.

Soft switching moves the device transition to a zero. Zero-voltage switching (ZVS) turns the device on only after its voltage has fallen to zero. Zero-current switching (ZCS) turns the device off only after its current has fallen to zero. In both cases the voltage-current overlap is removed, so the ½·V·I·t term for that transition goes to zero.

blocks.where: f_0 is the natural resonant frequency in hertz (Hz); L_r is the resonant inductance in henries (H); C_r is the resonant capacitance in farads (F). The tank exchanges energy at this frequency, and the switch is timed to its zero crossings.

blocks.text: For ZVS, a small resonant current flows before the gate pulse. It charges and discharges the device capacitance until the switch voltage reaches zero. Then the antiparallel body diode conducts and clamps the voltage at about zero. The gate pulse arrives while the diode is conducting, so the channel turns on with V ≈ 0. The body diode carries the current for that short wait.

For ZCS, the resonant inductor holds the current down. A resonant pulse brings the switch current to zero before the gate is removed. The device turns off with I = 0, and the voltage rises only afterwards. The price is a higher circulating current and a tank that must be tuned to the load.

A resonant converter replaces the PWM cell with a tank plus a switch. Four families cover most hardware. A series load-resonant converter puts the L-C tank in series with the load; the tank current is sinusoidal. A parallel load-resonant converter places the tank across the load; it can hold output at light load but carries more circulating current. A resonant-switch or quasi-resonant converter puts a small L_r and C_r around the switch, so the switch sees a zero crossing every cycle while the rest of the circuit still looks like a PWM cell. An LLC converter uses two inductors and one capacitor; it is common in laptop, phone and TV adapters because it gives ZVS on the primary switches.

The control variable changes. A buck sets V_o = D·V_s with duty ratio D; a resonant converter sets its gain by the ratio f_s/f_0. Moving f_s away from f_0 lowers the gain. The gain curve also depends on the tank quality factor Q, so at light load the usable range shrinks. This makes the regulation range narrower than a buck's: an LLC may hold output over a 2:1 input range, not from 0 to V_s.

Only a few universities derive the full gain curves. For most exams, know the loss comparison and the ZVS/ZCS definitions. If a paper asks for the gain, it usually gives the curve or asks for f_0 and the operating region.

figure.caption: The switch voltage is already 0 V when the gate pulse arrives at 2.5 µs, and the current is already 0 A when the voltage rises at 8 µs. This is zero-voltage turn-on and zero-current turn-off in a 10 µs period with 200 V and 5 A.

spec.aria: Timing diagram over 10 microseconds with three lanes: switch voltage, gate pulse, and switch current, showing voltage zero before gate on and current zero before voltage rise.

examples.question: A MOSFET in a hard-switched converter blocks 200 V and carries 5 A. It switches at 100 kHz. The voltage-current overlap times are t_r = 100 ns at turn-on and t_f = 100 ns at turn-off, and the overlap is triangular. The on-resistance is 0.1 Ω. Take 5 A as the rms device current for conduction. (a) Find the switching loss. (b) Find the conduction loss. (c) The circuit is changed to ZVS, which removes the turn-on overlap but leaves the turn-off overlap. Find the new total loss and compare with the hard-switched total.
steps: List the data: V = 200 V, I = 5 A, f_s = 100 kHz = 1×10⁵ Hz, t_r = 100 ns = 1×10⁻⁷ s, t_f = 100 ns = 1×10⁻⁷ s, R_on = 0.1 Ω.
Switching loss: P_sw = ½ × V × I × (t_r + t_f) × f_s. First V × I = 200 × 5 = 1000 W. Then t_r + t_f = 200 ns = 2×10⁻⁷ s. So P_sw = ½ × 1000 × 2×10⁻⁷ × 1×10⁵ = 10 W.
Conduction loss: P_cond = I² × R_on = 5² × 0.1 = 25 × 0.1 = 2.5 W.
Hard-switched total: P_total = P_sw + P_cond = 10 + 2.5 = 12.5 W.
With ZVS the turn-on overlap t_r is removed. Only turn-off overlap remains: P_off = ½ × V × I × t_f × f_s = ½ × 200 × 5 × 1×10⁻⁷ × 1×10⁵ = 5 W.
New total: P_ZVS = P_off + P_cond = 5 + 2.5 = 7.5 W. The saving is 5 W, or 40 % of the hard-switched loss.
examples.answer: P_sw = 10 W, P_cond = 2.5 W, and after ZVS the total falls from 12.5 W to 7.5 W.

traps: Using V·I·t·f_s without the ½ doubles the switching loss. The ½ comes from the triangular overlap, not from a duty ratio.
ZVS removes the turn-on overlap, not the conduction loss. The MOSFET still carries current, so I²R_on stays.
ZCS is a turn-off condition. It does not make the switch carry zero current during the on-time, and it does not clamp the off-state voltage to zero.
The tank frequency is 1/(2π√(L_r C_r)), not 1/√(L_r C_r). Missing 2π gives an answer in rad/s.
A resonant converter's gain is not D·V_s. Do not use the buck formula when the control variable is switching frequency.

quiz.q: Define zero-voltage switching (ZVS) and zero-current switching (ZCS) in one line each.
quiz.a: ZVS turns a device on only after its voltage has reached zero. ZCS turns a device off only after its current has reached zero.

quiz.q: Why does the total loss of a hard-switched converter have a minimum as switching frequency rises?
quiz.a: Conduction loss is set by current and R_on and stays roughly flat. Switching loss, diode recovery loss and C_oss loss grow with f_s. Once the switching terms exceed the saving from smaller magnetics, extra frequency only adds heat. The total therefore bottoms out at a best frequency.

quiz.q: A MOSFET has V = 100 V, I = 4 A, t_r = 50 ns, t_f = 80 ns and f_s = 200 kHz. Find the switching loss.
A resonant tank has L_r = 10 µH and C_r = 100 nF. Find f_0.
In the figure the gate pulse arrives at 2.5 µs, but the switch voltage has already reached 0 V at 2 µs. What makes the voltage zero, and why is this ZVS?
quiz.a: A resonant current charges and discharges C_oss until the switch voltage reaches zero. The body diode then conducts and clamps the voltage near zero. The gate pulse arrives while the diode holds V ≈ 0, so the channel turns on without voltage-current overlap. That is ZVS.

quiz.q: Why is the regulation range of an LLC converter narrower than that of a buck converter?
quiz.a: The LLC gain is set by f_s/f_0 and the tank quality factor Q, not by duty ratio. Moving f_s far from resonance lowers the gain and limits power. At light load Q is small and the gain curve flattens. A buck can use any duty from 0 to 1, but an LLC needs a frequency window and a tank designed for the load.

quiz.q: What is the role of the body diode in ZVS?
quiz.a: Before the gate pulse, the resonant current charges and discharges C_oss. When the voltage reaches zero, the body diode conducts and clamps it. The gate pulse can then arrive while the diode holds V near zero, so the channel turns on at zero voltage.

beyond: Not for the exam. LLC and series-resonant converters run at 100 kHz to over 1 MHz in phone chargers, TV supplies, server power and EV onboard chargers. Wide-bandgap GaN and SiC devices make those frequencies practical, and phase-shifted full-bridge designs use ZVS on the primary side. Search for LLC resonant converter gain curves, ZVS phase-shifted full bridge, and resonant switched-capacitor converters.
